```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)
library(knitr)
```

## ARIMA vs. ETS

### 2.1 The data

##### 2.1a read in the data
```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
```

##### 2.1b plot the data
```{r}
sales_plot <- liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly US liquor sales",
    x = "Year", y = "Sales (millions of dollars)"
  )

sales_plot

sales_seasonal_plot <- liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal plot of monthly US liquor sales",
    x = "Month", y = "Log Sales"
  )

sales_seasonal_plot
```
There's clear trend and seasonal pattern in the series. The series is overall trending upward each year and it also has a strong seasonal component. It has got an annual pattern in which the sales are highest in December and lowest in January. 
Since the series is trending upward and the seasonal swings do grow with the level of the series, we should use log transformation to stabilize the variance.

### 2.2 Fit Both Models

##### 2.2a fit ARIMA and ETS models
```{r}
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

The ARIMA model is ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1) with a seasonal period of 12, and the ETS model is ETS(A,A,A), an additive Holt-Winters model.
The ARIMA model gets one seasonal difference and no regular difference. The ETS model has an additive error component, an additive trend component and an additive seasonality component.

##### 2.2b ljung-box test for residuals in ARIMA model
```{r}
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 1+2+2+1)
```
The residuals do somewhat look like white noise, but by observing the ACF we could see that the series can be significantly correlated  with some seasonal lags. 
The Ljung-Box test also shows that the p-value is essentially 0, which is less than 0.05, indicating that the residuals are not white noise.

### 2.3 The Horse Race

##### 2.3a expanding-window TS-CV
```{r}
liquor_cv <- liquor |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 120, .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id))

liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")
```
There will be 216 forecast origins in total. The first forecast origin will be December 2001, and the last forecast origin will be November 2019. 

##### 2.3b produce one-month-ahead forecasts and compute accuracy
```{r}
liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) 
```
The first forecast will be January 2002, and the last forecast will be December 2019. 

```{r}
liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
The ARIMA model has the lowest RMSE and MAE, indicating that it forecasts most accurately among the three models. The two metrics agree.

### 2.4 Are the Differences Significant?

##### ARIMA v. ETS
```{r}
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)
```

##### ARIMA v. SNAIVE
```{r}
forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)
```

For the comparison between ARIMA and ETS, the DM statistic is -2.91 with its absolute value larger than 1.96. Thee p-value is 0.004, which is less than 0.05.
For the comparison between ARIMA and SNAIVE, the DM statistic is -10.76 with its absolute value larger than 1.96. The p-value is less than 2.2e-16, which is far less than 0.05.
Both DM tests' results indicate that the ARIMA model is making better forecasts and the difference in forecast accuracy between the two models is statistically significant. In other words, the ARIMA model is significantly more accurate than the ETS and SNAIVE models.
If I were the liquor store chain, I will use the ARIMA model to forecast the monthly liquor sales in the future.


## Forecast Combination

##### 3a. equal weight combination of ARIMA and ETS
```{r}
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE))

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```
The combination, with larger RMSE and MAE, does not beat the ARIMA model. It does beat ETS that goes into it as well as the seasonal random walk model.

##### 3b. correlation between forecast errors in models
```{r}
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```
There is a high positive correlation of 0.88 between the forecast errors of the ARIMA and ETS models. This indicates that the two models tend to make similar errors in their forecasts, which can limit the benefits of combining them from the very beginning. Additionally, the DM test says ARIMA is significantly better than ETS. The RMSE in the table also confirms that ETS is performing substantively worse than ARIMA. In this sense, it is reasonable that the equal weight combination does not beat the ARIMA model since the equal weighting will pull the performance of the combination down away from the level of the better model.


## VAR vs. BVAR

##### 4.1a read in data
```{r}
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))
```

##### 4.1b process data
```{r}
growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

nrow(y)
head(y)
```

##### 4.1c set up the TS-CV
```{r}
N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
```
We will be producing 120 forecasts for each variable. The date of the first forecast will be 1990 Q1 (shown as 1990-03-01) and the date of the last forecast will be 2019 Q4 (shown as 2019-12-01).

##### 4.2. OLS VARs
```{r}
var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}


rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
```
The VAR(1) has a smaller RMSE for 7 out of 8 variables, meaning that it forecasts better than VAR(4). Since the VAR(1) is basically a form of VAR(4) when the coefficient for all the latter three lags equals to 0 (an extreme form of the shrinkage we talked about in class), the difference between the two models are the excessive lag parameters. The key is that the redundant parameters in the VAR(4) could bring more in-sample fitting while risking overfitting the model, bringing more noise into the model. Thus, the out-of-sample forecast could perform worse with the estimation errors and noise carried along.

##### 4.3. A BVAR
```{r}
fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")
readRDS("results/var_results.rds") 
```
The BVAR(4) with lamba equals to 0.3 has smaller RMSE for all the variables than OLS VAR(4). This means that with the shrinkage, the BVAR with same number of variables and lags as an OLS VAR can tackle the overfitting problem to some extent.
The BVAR(4) with lamba equals to 0.3 has smaller RMSE for 3 out of 8 variables than OLS VAR(1) model. This means that the smaller number of lags included in the VAR(1) can also be helpful to tackle the overfitting problem.
When lambda equals to 0.05, our prior becomes much tighter, suggesting that we are more confident in that guess. Thus, the shrinkage becomes heavier with every lag coefficient getting pulled close to its prior mean of zero, which would be close to a simple benchmark mean model.
It would not be a fair estimate of how accurately it will forecast in the future. A fair estimate would require testing the chosen model on some new pseudo out-of-sample data and we also need a DM-test to confirm the statistical significance of the difference between the models. 

##### 4.3c DM-test
```{r}
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

e_var4 <- actual[, "unrate"] - fc_var4[, 6]
e_bvar <- actual[, "unrate"] - fc_bvar_03[, 6]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)
```
Both dm-test results suggest that, for GDP growth and unemployment rate, forecast produced by the BVAR(4) with lambda equals to 0.3 is performing better than the OLS VAR(4) model at either the 5% or 10% level.  
This suggests that shrinkage does help to tackle the problem brought by adding parameters. However, at the mean time, there are some uncertainty. Since many of the differences are small and not necessarily statitically significant, reading the rakings in that table should be more cautious.


## Factor Model

### 5.1. the data
```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```
The "INDPRO" and "PAYEMS" are both transformed into growth rate, the "CPIAUCSL" is transformed into change in the growth rate, the "FEDFUNDS" is transformed into first difference. 
The "INDPRO" may be a series of its own level trending upward while the "FEDFUNDS" being a series of growth rate with a trend. 
In this sense, the results would be more informative and easier to interpret after taking logs of the "INDPRO" and first difference of the "FEDFUNDS".

### 5.2. estimate the factors

##### 5.2a.
```{r}
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```
The first three factors explain 29.5% of the variation in all 121 series.  

##### 5.2b.
```{r}
F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

##### 5.2c.
```{r}
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```
The first factor might be a real activity factor since it falls sharply in every recession with high correlation with employment and industrial production.
The second factor might be an inflation factor with a high correaltion with the change in CPI inflation.

### 5.3. Replicate the Horse Race from Class
```{r}
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```
To estimate the factors once, using the full sample, and then use those in the horse race is cheating because it causes information leakage. The factors are estimated using the information from the full sample, which includes the future information that we are not supposed to know standing at the forecast origin in the TS-CV. This might lead to overly optimistic results and does not reflect the true out-of-sample forecasting performance of the model.

##### 5.4. a direct forecast of inflation
```{r}
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
```
The factors improve the forecast of 12-month CPI inflation. It reduces the RMSE by 10.4%. The difference is also statistically significant because the p-value of the DM test is much less than 0.05. This suggests that the factor-augmented model provides a significantly better forecast of inflation than the simple AR model.


## Reflection
Across the horse races of models, simple models are hard to beat if the data is limited, which might be most of time in practice. Since every additional estimated parameters adds estimation error and noise to the model, simple models perform well because of their parsimony in parameters. Notably, too simple or too much shrinkage can also be harmful since they cannot really capture more informative underlying patterns in the data, as seen in the failure of SNAIVE model and the BVAR(4) with lambda equals to 0.05.

One idea that appeared repeatedly is that shrinkage, equal-weight combination, and factors are different ways to tackle the tradeoff between adding more parameters into the estimation and the risk of overfitting. Shrinkage pulls coefficients toward zero to make truly informative parameters flesh out. For those equally accurate models, equal-weight combination aims to avoid estimation noise based on a limited number of past forecast errors by weighting different models equally. Factors compress large amount of data from numerous series into a smaller number of components. All of them are trying to reduce effect of the estimation errors and noise brought by adding parameters on forecast accuracy. 

Another recurring idea is that RMSE rankings alone are not enough, and DM tests are needed to judge whether differences in accuracy are statistically meaningful or just noise. Finally, every evaluation had to avoid information leakage by using only data available at each forecast origin, whether in the expanding-window TS-CV or when re-estimating the factors. Overall, good forecasting is about an elegant balance - using the useful information as much as possible without overfitting.
